analyst_note: Events 9–11 show an admin01 remote-interactive logon from localhost, accompanied by standard Windows session components (15–19). The rundll32 launch (12) lacks command-line or parent details indicating misuse; the supplied events do not establish malicious activity.

The IIS worker process repeatedly connects to local RDP (events 0, 2) and SMB (events 6, 8). This unusual access to administrative services suggests an IIS-hosted tunnel or proxy rather than normal web-serving activity.

Windows service and System connections to private or loopback addresses are consistent with routine service traffic (events 0, 3, 10, 15). Event 19 shows System32\taskhost.exe launched by services.exe as LOCAL SERVICE, with no clear malicious behavior in the supplied telemetry.
ProcDump and ProcDump64 accessed lsass.exe with full process rights (0x001fffff) in events 0, 1, and 2. This is consistent with LSASS credential-dumping activity, although dump creation is not shown.

Events 0, 1, and 4–6 show machine-account network logons from loopback; events 2–3 show anonymous network logons from an internal IP. These authentication events alone provide insufficient evidence of malicious activity.

The suspicious double-extension executable voice_mail.msg.exe obtained all-access permissions to LSASS (7) and created remote threads inside it (2, 8). This indicates LSASS injection consistent with credential-access activity, although credential extraction is not directly shown.

Events 0–1 and 3–4 show Administrator network logons and IPC$ eventlog access from 172.16.66.37, consistent with remote event-log administration. Event 2 records a SYSTEM service logon; the supplied events contain no clear evidence of malicious activity.

RDP Wrapper redirects TermService to rdpwrap.dll, enables RDP and concurrent sessions, and opens inbound TCP 3389 (7–11). The patcher invokes ownership and Everyone full-control changes on termsrv.dll (14,16), while RDP's listening port is changed to 80 (17), supporting persistent remote-access setup.

CDPSvc was stopped and restarted (0, 3), and svchost.exe loaded cdpsgshims.dll from the nonstandard Chocolatey bin directory (5), consistent with service DLL hijacking. A SYSTEM-level whoami execution (6) and netcat connection to localhost:1337 (7) further support malicious privilege-escalation activity.

Events 0–2 show user01 from 10.0.2.17 accessing the winreg, lsarpc, and srvsvc named pipes through IPC$. This combination is consistent with SMB/RPC reconnaissance targeting registry, account, and share information.

Events 2–8 show user01 from 10.0.2.17 repeatedly accessing SAMR, LSARPC, NETLOGON, and SRVSVC through IPC$. This concentrated, multi-interface pattern is consistent with remote account, domain, and share enumeration.

PowerShell made repeated LDAP connections to 10.59.4.11 under a domain Administrator account (0–1). The accompanying SMB fan-out to seven internal hosts (2–8) suggests automated Active Directory and network discovery.

The ProgramData copy of vshadow.exe uses -exec to target OSK and Notepad, with Notepad child execution confirmed (0, 2, 3). OSK also runs under Utilman.exe /debug (1), reinforcing the suspicious LOLBin execution pattern.

Event 1 shows cmd.exe using pcalua.exe with -a to indirectly launch calc.exe; event 2 confirms execution. This unusual compatibility-utility invocation is consistent with LOLBin-based indirect execution for defense evasion.

WinPwnage created a temporary URL file and abused rundll32.exe with ieframe.dll,OpenURL to launch cmd.exe (events 0–3). A subsequent rundll32 URL-handler invocation launched an HTA through mshta.exe, which spawned calc.exe, demonstrating trusted-binary proxy execution (events 8–10).

PowerShell loaded taskschd.dll (0) and connected to 10.0.2.17 on RPC port 135 and dynamic port 49666 (1–2). This combination suggests remote scheduled-task activity for lateral movement, although task creation or execution is not confirmed.

PowerShell server mode is associated with loopback SMB activity, a user03 network logon, and access to the custom IPC$ pipe 'samir' (0–2, 4). The server launches cmd.exe as user03 rather than IEUser (3), consistent with SMB/named-pipe remote execution using alternate credentials.

PowerShell launched command shells and connected to 10.0.2.18:38208 (2, 4, 6). Combined with netstat, whoami, and systeminfo execution (0, 7, 8), this pattern is consistent with shell-driven post-compromise discovery.

Events 0–1 register a file in the user's Documents folder as an in-process COM server. Event 2 redirects another CLSID to that server through TreatAs, consistent with COM hijacking for persistence; payload execution is not shown.

Utilman.exe launched by winlogon.exe executes C:\osk.exe from an abnormal location, consistent with accessibility-feature hijacking for privilege escalation (events 14, 16). Explorer also launches the PsExec service component PSEXESVC.exe, adding suspicious remote-administration activity (event 9).

MSBuild.exe modified the protected SAM record for RID 501 (Guest), an anomalous action consistent with account tampering for privilege escalation (0). PsExec EULA acceptance and PSEXESVC service configuration additionally indicate remote-administration tooling setup (1–3).

UACME.exe launched eventvwr.exe, followed by consent.exe loading comctl32.dll from a suspicious .local DLL-redirection path (0, 2, 4, 8). consent.exe then spawned command shells as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, demonstrating successful privilege escalation through a UAC-bypass chain (5, 9).

UACME.exe ran with method 53 (0), and the per-user Folder shell-open handler was set to cmd.exe with an empty DelegateExecute value (2,4). The subsequent sdclt.exe → control.exe → cmd.exe chain (5,7,8) indicates a UAC-bypass privilege-escalation attempt.

UACME.exe executed method 33 [0], and the ms-settings registry handler was set to cmd.exe with an empty DelegateExecute value [1,2]. UACME then launched fodhelper.exe, which spawned cmd.exe [3,5], indicating a UAC-bypass privilege-escalation chain.

Outlook launched from Explorer and made an HTTPS connection consistent with normal email activity (events 0–1). Excel opened a local .xlsx workbook from Explorer, with no suspicious commands or child processes shown (event 2).

GoogleUpdate.exe starts through services.exe as SYSTEM (0), connects over HTTPS (1), and writes a Chrome installer to its update download directory (2). These events are consistent with a routine Google Chrome update.

The svc_backup service logon (0) and wbadmin command backing up C: to E: (1) are consistent with routine backup activity. Creation of metadata under WindowsImageBackup (2) supports a legitimate backup operation.

VS Code launched a Git pull and a Python pytest run, consistent with normal development activity (events 0 and 2). Git's HTTPS helper connected on port 443, consistent with fetching repository updates (event 1).
